subject: Communication
title: Nonviolent Communication (NVC)
description: Learn Nonviolent Communication (NVC) in one minute.

hook.text: Marshall Rosenberg walked into a room of warring factions in the Middle East armed with one framework. No weapons.

buildup.text: NVC has four steps: observe without evaluating, state feelings, identify needs, and make a clear request.

discovery.text: 'You never listen' becomes 'When I see you on your phone during our talks, I feel hurt because I need connection.'

twist.text: NVC sounds mechanical at first. But it works because it replaces blame language with ownership language.

climax.text: Rosenberg used NVC in prisons, war zones, and schools. The framework scales from personal arguments to international peace.

punchline.text: Violence starts with language. So does peace.

quiz.question: What are the four steps of Nonviolent Communication?

details.summary: Marshall Rosenberg's Nonviolent Communication framework uses four steps: observe without evaluating, state your feeling, identify your need, and make a clear request. NVC transforms adversarial exchanges into conversations about universal human needs.
details.whyItMatters: NVC provides a concrete script for turning blame and defensiveness into understanding, making it one of the most practical conflict resolution tools.
takeaways: Four steps: observation, feeling, need, request
NVC focuses on universal human needs beneath conflict

faq.question: Does NVC sound awkward in real conversations?
faq.answer: The formal four-step structure can feel scripted initially. With practice, it becomes natural. The key is internalizing the mindset of curiosity about needs rather than reciting the formula mechanically. Most practitioners adapt the language to fit their personality.

faq.question: What is the difference between a request and a demand in NVC?
faq.answer: A request allows the other person to say no without punishment. A demand implies consequences for refusal. NVC emphasizes that true requests include willingness to hear alternatives and continue dialogue. If no is not acceptable, it is a demand disguised as a request.
